original_question: For new noncommutative cryptographic schemes such as public-key exchange, digital signatures, and authentication, how can one prove that a chosen group platform is secure?
target_in_paper: Section 11, General open problem 3: "How can we show a group is provably secure for the new non-commutative schemes such as public key exchanges, digital signatures and authentication?" ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1103.4093))
correct_elements: Your draft is very close to the paper’s own formulation. It correctly targets the open problem about proving security of a non-commutative group platform, and it preserves the same three application classes named in the paper: public key exchange, digital signatures, and authentication. It also keeps the focus on platform security rather than drifting to a broader question about inventing new primitives. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1103.4093))
missing_details: The paper presents this as an open problem in its final list, not as a theorem, conjecture, or already-formalized security statement. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1103.4093))

The relevant object is a non-commutative group used as a platform group; in the surveyed schemes this is typically a finitely presented group given by a group presentation. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1103.4093))

Nearby sections make implicit platform assumptions that your draft does not state: one wants usable or unique normal forms, efficient computation of those normal forms, and a solvable word problem. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1103.4093))

For several protocols the paper also assumes that normal forms of products should not reveal the hidden factors, so platform security is tied to how elements are represented. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1103.4093))

The hard problem is scheme-dependent: conjugator search for Anshel-Anshel-Goldfeld, conjugacy or search conjugacy for Ko-Lee and related exchange schemes, and search-conjugacy-type hardness for the signature scheme. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1103.4093))

For authentication/password-verification, the paper points to different assumptions, including hardness of solving the word problem without the hidden presentation and hardness of systems of equations in free groups; it also cites one challenge-response method as provably secure against ciphertext-only, man-in-the-middle, and replay attacks. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1103.4093))

For Ko-Lee-type exchange and related key-transport schemes, large commuting subgroups are additionally required, so a 'secure platform group' is partly protocol-specific. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1103.4093))

Section 7 adds further candidate-platform criteria omitted by the draft: a large key space via exponential growth and, ideally, exponential-time complexity of the conjugator search problem. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1103.4093))

The paper does not fix one formal meaning of 'provably secure'; Open Problem 6 explicitly asks what the right security measure should be: practicality, worst-case complexity, average-case complexity, or generic complexity. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1103.4093))

Sections 9-10 show why generic behavior matters: braid groups can have the strong generic free group property, so random subgroup choices may be vulnerable even when worst-case hardness looks promising. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1103.4093))
refined_question: In the setting of the non-commutative group-based cryptosystems surveyed in this paper, how can one formulate rigorous criteria and proof methods showing that a candidate nonabelian platform group G is provably secure for the specific schemes considered here—public-key exchange, digital signatures, and authentication/password-verification—where G is used via a finite presentation with efficiently computable normal forms and solvable word problem, the relevant scheme-specific hard problems (such as conjugator/conjugacy search or the authentication-related word-problem/equation-solving attacks) are infeasible, any required large commuting subgroups exist, and the security proof is evaluated in the appropriate sense (practical, worst-case, average-case, or generic-case)? ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1103.4093))
justification: The draft almost reproduces the paper’s own Section 11 wording, so the target is clear. I sharpened it only by importing the nearby assumptions that the paper treats as implicit when speaking about platform groups and security: finitely presented/nonabelian group platforms with effective normal forms and solvable word problem for exchange protocols, scheme-dependent hardness assumptions for signatures and authentication, and the paper’s own insistence that security analysis must account for generic and average-case behavior because many proposed platform groups—especially braid groups—exhibit strong generic free-subgroup phenomena. Since the paper gives no explicit equivalence or alternate formal statement for Open Problem 3, no alternate formulation should be invented. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1103.4093))
